blind.location: Printed p. 84 (source page 6), Problem 2
blind.quote:
Problem 2. Alice typically scores around 80 on weekly 100-point quizzes in one
     of her classes. One week she sets a goal of scoring 90. She scores 87.
       Betty typically scores around 80 on weekly 100-point quizzes in one of her classes.
     One week she decides to do her best. She scores 83.
       Overall, who will be more satisfied with her performance? [N ⫽ 60]

   Both Alice and Betty typically perform at the same level on their weekly
quizzes, and this week both have exceeded their typical score. Thus if they
used their normal performance as their reference point, both should be happy
but Alice should be happier. However, because goals operate as reference
points, Alice ends up in the domain of losses because she performs three
points below her reference point. Although Alice performs above Betty in
absolute terms, people agree that she will be less satisfied with her perfor-
mance ( p ⬍ .05 by χ 2 ).

At 42 sit-ups, the slopes of the two value functions indicate that Charles
receives lower benefits from an additional sit-up than David. Note that

to his goal and experiencing smaller effects of diminishing sensitivity, to
exert more effort after the 42nd sit-up (p ⬍ .05 by χ 2 ).

blind.location: Printed p. 90 (source page 12), Problem 7
blind.quote:
Problem 7 successfully distinguishes the value function approach from
the traditional goal-setting approach. When Charles and David are both be-
low their goals, the value function in Fig. 2 clearly predicts that Charles will
exert more effort than David at 28 sit-ups because he receives higher benefits.
Again, this prediction follows from diminishing sensitivity, Charles is closer
to his goal and is much more sensitive to movements toward it, b′30 (28) ⫽
v′(⫺2) ⬎ v′(⫺12) ⫽ b′40 (28). Consistent with the value function prediction
but not goal setting, participants expected Charles to exert more effort after
the 28th sit-up (p ⬍ .001 by χ 2 ).

blind.location: Printed p. 91 (source page 13), Problem 8
blind.quote:
Problem 8. [N ⫽ 47] Jim decides that he would like to donate more time to charity.
    His schedule won’t permit more than 4 h per week, so he sets a personal goal of
    working 40 h over the next 10 weeks at a neighborhood soup kitchen. Soon after
    starting, Jim learns that the soup kitchen will be forced to close in 4 weeks.
       Kyle decides that he would like to donate more time to charity. His schedule
    won’t permit more than 4 h per week, so he sets a personal goal of working 200 h
    over the next year at a neighborhood soup kitchen. Soon after starting, Kyle learns
    that the soup kitchen will be forced to close in 4 weeks.
       Who will donate more time to the soup kitchen over the next 4 weeks?
       Please circle one Jim (81%) Kyle (19%)

   Note that Jim and Kyle have set goals that require them to work at a
similar rate (4 h per week). Also note that neither will reach his goal before
the soup kitchen closes. However, according to the value function, Jim feels
that he is making more progress than Kyle: b40 (16) ⫽ v(⫺24) ⫺ v(⫺40) ⬎
v(⫺184) ⫺ v(⫺200) ⫽ b200 (16). Consistent with the notion of a ‘‘starting
problem,’’ people feel that Kyle will find it more difficult to start working
toward his high goal.

disposition.reason: Problem 8 gives Jim 81%, Kyle 19%, and a qualitative starting-problem interpretation; no numeric test statistic or p value is printed.

worker_notes:
Original side is an unassigned placeholder, not an assessment of original-source availability. Every assigned row has a blank description; study 1 and a page locator do not distinguish the critical predictor/outcome/test. Candidate common model N is documented directly, not derived: 2968 students; 882 teachers; 480 schools. No arithmetic performed. Continuous-variable standardisation is explicitly documented on p. 7: We standardized all continuous variables in the analysis (M = 0, SD = 1). This does not establish that every categorical coefficient is a fully standardised beta. Page 8 reading narrative candidate coefficient/p pairs (same-test pairs, not assigned): reading methods-course school average gamma500=-0.30, p=0.04; school SES gamma700=0.03, p=0.05; prior achievement beta100=0.74, p<.001; elapsed time beta200=0.10, p<.001; student SES beta300=0.04, p=.006; gender beta500=0.12, p<.001. Page 8 Table 3 also contains school/teacher/student random variances (.06/.08/.87 for reading; .01/.11/.88 for mathematics), ICCs and reliability estimates; these are distinct metrics and tests. Page 9 mathematics narrative candidate coefficient/p pairs (same-test pairs, not assigned): beta100=0.76, p<.001; beta200=0.06, p<.001; beta300=0.05, p=.004; beta500=-0.15, p<.001. The narrative labels beta100 previous reading achievement but its interpretation and Table 4 identify prior mathematics achievement; retain this source inconsistency. Table 4 pp. 9–10 provides multiple school-, teacher-, and student-level estimates for both outcomes with SEs and a p<.05 star legend, rather than exact p for every coefficient. blind.quote: As predicted, the postextinction administration of l -DOPA compared to placebo (see Fig. 1a ) enhanced extinction memory retrieval and reduced the expression of fear at test on day 3 (stimulus: F 1,33 = 44.61, P < .001, partial η 2 = 0.58, stimulus × group: F 1,33 = 6.58, P = 0.02, partial η 2 = 0.17; n = 35; Fig. 1b ). ... g The postextinction administration of l -DOPA had a significant positive effect on number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations (path a: ß = 0.97, SE = 0.30, T 33 = 3.23, P = 0.003; n = 35). The number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations 45 min after extinction was significantly negatively related to smaller differential CRs at test on day 3 (path b: β = −0.10, SE = 0.03, T 33 = −4.26, P = 0.0002; n = 35). After inclusion of number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations into the latter model, the significant effect of drug on CRs at test (path c: ß = −0.15, SE = 0.06, T 33 = −2.57, P = 0.02; n = 35) decreased (path c’: β = −0.06, SE = 0.06, T 32 = −0.98, P = 0.33; n = 35), indicating that the effect of l -DOPA on CRs at test on day 3 was significantly mediated (c–c’ = −0.09, 95% CI: −0.13 to −0.02, P = 0.007; bootstrapping procedure with 10,000 simulations; n = 35) by number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations 45 min after extinction ... Intriguingly, the number of reactivations of the CS+ offset-related vmPFC pattern at 45 min postextinction mediated the effect of l -DOPA on CRs at test (Fig. 2g ; mediation analysis—indirect mediator effect: β = −0.09, 95% CI: −0.13 to −0.02, P = 0.007; bootstrapping procedure with 10,000 simulations; n = 35).

blind.quote:
In phase 0, the control group rated bad items
significantly lower than the intervention group, estimated difference = −0.261, 95%
CI = [−0.456, −0.0653], p = .009. Nevertheless, in phase 1 the control group rated bad items
significantly higher than the intervention group, estimated difference = 0.525, 95% CI = [0.328,
0.722], p < .0001, and phase 2, estimated difference = 0.543, 95% CI = [0.349, 0.7362], p < .0001.
The third column in Table 3 shows the model parameters for predictors group by phase on
knowledge application ratings for each good quality item as a dependent variable. There were no
significant differences between groups for the good items in phase 0 or in phase 2, ps > .05; but
in phase 1 the control group rated good items significantly lower than the intervention group,
estimated difference = −0.2589, 95% CI = [−0.448, −0.07], p = .0073. There were no significant
differences between the ratings in each phase in the control group or in the intervention group,
ps > .05.

blind.location: p.274 Discussion and RQ1 discussion
blind.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

blind.location: p.266, pairwise contrast results beneath Table 3
blind.quote:
In phase 0, the control group rated bad items
significantly lower than the intervention group, estimated difference = −0.261, 95%
CI = [−0.456, −0.0653], p = .009. Nevertheless, in phase 1 the control group rated bad items
significantly higher than the intervention group, estimated difference = 0.525, 95% CI = [0.328,
0.722], p < .0001, and phase 2, estimated difference = 0.543, 95% CI = [0.349, 0.7362], p < .0001.
The third column in Table 3 shows the model parameters for predictors group by phase on
knowledge application ratings for each good quality item as a dependent variable. There were no
significant differences between groups for the good items in phase 0 or in phase 2, ps > .05; but
in phase 1 the control group rated good items significantly lower than the intervention group,
estimated difference = −0.2589, 95% CI = [−0.448, −0.07], p = .0073. There were no significant
differences between the ratings in each phase in the control group or in the intervention group,
ps > .05.

initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

blind.location: p.274 Discussion and RQ1 discussion
blind.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

blind.location: p.267, RQ2 Accuracy
blind.quote:
In phase 0, there were no significant differences between groups for
the text selection, estimated OR = 0.8563, 95% CI = [0.4040, 1.815], p = .6858. Nevertheless,
accuracy was higher after the intervention for the trained group: In both post-tests the control
group chose the more reliable text significantly less than the intervention group, phase 1:
estimated OR = 0.0588, 95% CI = [0.0174, 0.199], p < .0001; phase 2: estimated OR = 0.1601,
95% CI = [0.0626, 0.410], p = .0001.

blind.location: p.274 Discussion and RQ1 discussion
blind.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

worker_target_description: Kontkanen (2024), section 4.2.1 and Table 4 current-study ing column: chi-square comparison of progressive -ing TLU rates between beginners (A1+A2) and intermediates (B1+B2). Matching is based on the named morpheme and comparison, not numeric values.
worker_notes: Only n_r and reported_success were assigned; original, replication es and replication p are unassigned null placeholders. input.description: Article. The annotation covers OCs of (in)definite articles (a(n)/the). Given that the ‘zero article’ was disregarded in previous MOS, it was also disregarded here for comparative purposes. The non-suppliance of an article in an (in)definite OC was tagged as omission. Also, given that both definite and indefinite articles were analysed as a single morpheme in previous MOS, we analysed them similarly, even if we are aware that they are better analysed separately as they do not emerge simultaneously (cf. the discussion in Section 4.4). Selection of one article for the other was tagged as ‘mis-selection’. The forms a/an were understood as spelling variants, so selection of one when the other was expected was not tagged as NTLU. Importantly, determining the OC of the/a(n) is based on information-status distinctions deriving from discourse, i.e., on whether the entity has been previously mentioned in the discourse (i.e., discourse-old, topic) or not (i.e., discourse-new, focus), and therefore whether or not the referent is known to the reader. Articles were annotated independently of the appearance of characters in the picture story, which could give the sense of old information, but technically introduce discoursenew information when retelling the story to a reader. Therefore, ILA considers hearer/reader knowledge (and not speaker knowledge) to determine discourse-old/discourse-new distinctions (cf. Hawkins, 2001).
